title: Spain's rail authorities face European fraud probe after Urda rail disaster
description: European Union prosecutors have begun investigating the possible misuse of EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash k
body: European Union prosecutors have begun investigating the possible misuse of EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people last week.Prosecutors backed by a special unit of Spain's Guardia Civil security force said they were conducting the inquiry at the offices of Adif rail infrastructure authority and rail safety agency AESF.The 28 October accident on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line was one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century. It is the second EU fraud inquiry opened into Spain's railways this year, after 46 people were killed on the same line at Adamuz in January.Last week, a train operated by state-owned operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo outside the village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.The LZB communication system that monitors the position of trains had gone down, and the Renfe train had been given the all clear to start running at normal speed, even though the Iryo train ahead of it had been unable to restart.The two accidents nine months apart on the same line have claimed 115 lives and dozens more injuries.

schema.headline: Spain's rail authorities face European fraud probe after Urda rail disaster

title: Prince Harry and five others seek to challenge Mail publisher privacy ruling
description: The Duke of Sussex and five other high-profile figures who lost a privacy case against the publisher of the Daily Mail and Mail on Sunday are seeking
body: The Duke of Sussex and five other high-profile figures who lost a privacy case against the publisher of the Daily Mail and Mail on Sunday are seeking to challenge the High Court ruling.Prince Harry, singer Sir Elton John and actress Elizabeth Hurley were among the group facing paying joint legal costs of up to £34.5m after the court ruled in July they had failed to prove the allegations of unlawful information gathering. Associated Newspapers Limited strongly denied the claims, which were heard at an 11-week trial in London that ended with judge Mr Justice Nicklin dismissing all the allegations.At the time, a spokesperson for the publisher described the judgement as an "overwhelming victory for the Daily Mail and its journalists".The prince testified in person during the civil hearing and claimed the details that appeared in 14 articles about him "plainly" proved journalists were listening in to phone calls - but a High Court judge said he had failed to prove that.On Friday, a spokesperson for Prince Harry, Hurley, Sir Elton, his husband David Furnish, actress Sadie Frost and political campaigner Baroness Lawrence said the claimants had filed applications with the Court of Appeal applying for permission to challenge the judgements.The statement said the planned appeal was both on Mr Justice Nicklin's dismissal of their claims and a subsequent indemnity costs order.The spokesperson said: "The claimants respectfully disagree with those unprecedented decisions, which they consider to be legally and factually flawed."In August, a month on from his judgement, Mr Justice Nicklin ruled that the case was a rare one in which the claimants should have to pay far in excess of the costs that had been agreed before the trial.He also ordered at that time the claimants should make an initial payment of £9.54m while the final total was calculated.The statement from the group's joint spokesperson did not make any reference to Liberal Democrat politician Sir Simon Hughes who was part of the action. The BBC has contacted Sir Simon to establish whether he is joining the appeal.After the costs ruling, he told the BBC he was "disappointed" and would take "the  time necessary to consider both the substantive and the costs judgment and whether to pursue appeals against decisions in either judgment or both".The trial saw many current and former Mail and Mail on Sunday journalists and executives giving evidence denying accusations of illegal activity that was put to them by lawyers representing the prince and his fellow claimants.Lawyers for the publisher said in court that the journalists had provided a "compelling account of a pattern of legitimate sourcing of articles", including using information provided by friends and "leaky" social circles surrounding those they had written about.In a civil case such as this, the legal convention is that the losing party must reimburse "reasonable" legal fees incurred by the other side. They also have to settle their own legal costs.

schema.headline: Prince Harry and five others seek to challenge Mail publisher privacy ruling

title: Austrian police investigate man for leaving 17-year-old on Germany's highest mountain Zugspitze
description: The weather was so poor that the two climbers were soon knee-deep in snow, according to Austrian reports, and their plans to reach the 2,962m summit s
body: The weather was so poor that the two climbers were soon knee-deep in snow, according to Austrian reports, and their plans to reach the 2,962m summit soon changed.At one point they separated and the 21-year-old descended alone. The reason they split is unclear, and a police spokesperson declined to comment, citing the ongoing investigation.Seven mountain rescuers responded to the call, and a helicopter eventually airlifted the teenager off the mountain. She was then taken to hospital by ambulance.Although the teenager survived, what happened on Zugspitze on Sunday is reminiscent of a fatal incident on Austria's highest peak, the Grossglockner, in January 2025.A 33-year-old woman froze to death on the Grossglockner after her boyfriend left her on the mountain, and he was later found guilty of grossly negligent manslaughter.The boyfriend had insisted he had left her there while trying to get help, telling the court he had loved his girlfriend and that he was deeply sorry.The case reverberated throughout the mountaineering community at the time, with prosecutors arguing that as the more experienced climber, he was the responsible guide on the trip and had failed to turn back or call for help in time. In the latest case in Austria, police have said once they have completed their investigation, a report will be sent to Innsbruck public prosecutors, who will decide if a criminal offence has been committed.

schema.headline: Austrian police investigate man for leaving 17-year-old on Germany's highest mountain Zugspitze

title: Trump names Stephen Miller as new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles
description: One of Trump's closest aides, Miller stuck by the president following his 2020 election defeat and followed Trump back into power last year.Wiles gave
body: One of Trump's closest aides, Miller stuck by the president following his 2020 election defeat and followed Trump back into power last year.Wiles gave her resignation to Trump on Thursday night, a US official told CBS News, the BBC's media partner. Three sources told CBS she quit because of the election losses.Trump said in a statement that Wiles would be moved to the "Trump Political Operation". He told reporters that Miller "gets it, very good politically".Wiles said being on Trump's team was "the honor of a lifetime". "I'm so proud to have been a part of what we've accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First," she said. "While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will."It was unclear if her deputies would remain at the White House.Wiles, 69, is seen as among the most powerful figures in the Trump administration and someone particularly close to the US president.Asked last month whether Wiles could be replaced soon, Trump said there was "zero chance". "Susie is here and she's gonna be here for a long time," he said. Wiles recently battled cancer, announcing in September, six months after her diagnosis, that she was in remission. Wiles is not the only high-profile Trump official to leave this week following the midterm elections, which have prompted a reckoning among Republicans about how to address voters' rebuke of Trump's agenda. Several justice department officials have also resigned, including John Eisenberg, the head of the department's National Security Division, and Jason Reding Quiñones, who was known for enforcing conspiracy probes into officials investigating Trump's handling of classified documents.Democrats took to social media to criticise Trump's new pick, accusing him of doubling down despite voters' anger with his party's agenda. Democratic Congressman Robert Garcia, who would lead the House Oversight Committee after Democrats take control of the chamber, said he would continue to investigate Miller and his "misconduct". "Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families," he said, referencing US Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Democratic House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Miller was "a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands"."His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor," he said. Trump's communications director Steven Cheung called Miller "someone who has been with the President since the very beginning". "There is no bigger advocate for the Trump agenda than Stephen, and he will help the Administration deliver on monumental victories for the rest of this historic second term," he said.

schema.headline: Trump names Stephen Miller as new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles

title: Two dead after bus crashes in France, officials say
description: A young girl and an 18-year-old man have died after a bus crashed in eastern France, local authorities have said.The bus was travelling between Lyon a
body: A young girl and an 18-year-old man have died after a bus crashed in eastern France, local authorities have said.The bus was travelling between Lyon and Bourg-en-Bresse when it crashed at around 07:00 local time on Friday in the town of Lent.The bus was carrying 43 passengers, including 15 children, the Bourg-en-Bresse prosecutor's office said. Three people are in a critical condition and at least 13 others have sustained minor injuries.French President Emmanuel Macron said his thoughts were with the victims, the injured, and their families. In a post on X, he said the nation stood by their side and thanked the rescue teams involved.The town's mayor Yves Cristin told French media the bus "left the road and hit a tree in the ditch".The two people killed have been identified by authorities. However, there have been differing reports as to the age of the girl.The prosecutor's office said it was "opening an investigation into the incident, on charges of road homicide and aggravated road traffic injuries". The driver has been taken to hospital after sustaining injuries and has not yet been questioned by police. French Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot said initial tests indicated there were no traces of alcohol or drugs in his blood. Photos circulating in French media show a blue and white bus tilted in what appears to be a ditch on the roadside. Trees line the side of the road. The front of the bus appears to be heavily damaged.Local mayor Cristin told BFM TV: "I arrived minutes after the accident and people were in shock."The side of the bus was torn off, and clearly, the people who were on that side must have been seriously injured."Addressing weather conditions at the time of the crash, the mayor told Le Figaro "there was a bit of fog, the road was wet" but there were "no major difficulties". Speaking to the same paper, Fabrice Pannekoucke, head of the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region, said: "At this stage, there are no particular explanations or interpretations that can be given."Tabarot said the bus did not operate "exclusively on school routes" but that there were "many schoolchildren on board".

schema.headline: Two dead after bus crashes in France, officials say

title: Spate of bomb threats poses serious challenge to airline industry
description: All this poses a serious challenge to the airlines, who have little idea who is causing the severe disruption they have faced almost every day this we
body: All this poses a serious challenge to the airlines, who have little idea who is causing the severe disruption they have faced almost every day this week.Although so far all threats have turned out to be hoaxes, airlines have no choice but take each threat seriously."They have a triage system, but follow the same protocols for each until they are absolutely sure there is no threat," says Marco Chan, a former commercial airline pilot and aviation expert at Kingston University."That could involve a mid-air inspection, but definitely a search once the plane has landed."Passengers might not even know there is an issue until they are told to disembark. It can cause disruption, but that is a small price to pay when safety is at stake", he adds.The sight of sniffer dogs and specialist teams on the tarmac searching for explosives on commercial planes may cause alarm.So far, the disruption too has been limited to the few thousand passengers who have been directly involved.Paul Mason, an aviation security expert, says there will be a financial cost to the airline involved, but planes get diverted every day."The number can sometimes run to over a hundred planes daily, for things like technical issues, medical emergencies, even the weather," he adds. "They far outweigh the few which have been diverted due to hoaxes. So airlines are well equipped at dealing with the unexpected."It is also unlikely that customers will be able to get refunds, he explains, because these incidents are not the fault of the airlines.The more worrying aspect over the past few days will be the seeming random nature of the targets and the lack of any credible intelligence regarding who is behind the threats.Aside from emails suggesting that an extremist misogynist group had claimed responsibility for a handful of the incidents - although since denied by its founder - there appear to be few leads.With 20 years of military experience as well, Paul Mason says the incidents bear the hallmarks of hybrid warfare, which involves unconventional methods such as cyber attacks."It does feel co-ordinated," he says. "Russia has said it's got nothing to do with it, but it could be proxies. It's a very easy way to create disruption and chaos, with plausible deniability.""That's the problem. Someone can have an opinion on who is behind it, but if the perpetrators are using sophisticated technology, it will be very hard to trace them."He does say however that if misguided individuals try to copy the threats they could find themselves in serious trouble.The Aviation Security Act 1982 states that "intentionally communicating false, misleading, or deceptive information that endangers - or is likely to endanger - the safety of an aircraft in flight is a serious criminal offense".The maximum sentence is life imprisonment.There is precious little that airports and airlines can do to guard against actually receiving threats, as they can come from a vast range of sources. But the punishment is designed to act as a deterrent.As Paul Mason warns: "Someone might think it's a laugh and very easy to do, but unless they are very sophisticated, they are highly likely to be traced. And find themselves facing prison."

schema.headline: Spate of bomb threats poses serious challenge to airline industry

title: Brand's barrister refers himself to regulator after report he confronted journalist
description: Russell Brand's defence barrister has referred himself to the regulator after reports that he confronted a Sunday Times journalist who was involved in
body: Russell Brand's defence barrister has referred himself to the regulator after reports that he confronted a Sunday Times journalist who was involved in a media investigation into Brand in 2023.In a Times and Sunday Times podcast on Thursday, Rosamund Urwin said she introduced herself to Ian Winter KC outside court after verdicts were delivered.She claimed he responded with a "snarl" and said "I hope you're pleased with yourself"."Apparently I said, but I can't actually remember this but I've read it in reporting, 'I am pleased that justice has been done'", Urwin said.She said that Winter replied "it wasn't" and suggested she was to blame using a profanity.In a statement, Winter said the "ways matters have been characterised" in the media  meant they should be "subject to proper scrutiny".On Friday, Winter said he considered his professional duty required him to self-report the allegations to the Bar Standards Board.The Bar Standards Board regulates barristers in England and Wales in the public interest.In a statement, Winter said: "Having seen the ways matters have been characterised in today's press I consider my professional duty requires me to self-report those allegations to the Bar Standards Board, so the matter can be subject to proper scrutiny. I have made such a report."Four women variously accused Brand of rape, sexual assaults and emotional abuse in a joint investigation by Channel 4 Dispatches and the Times and Sunday Times in September 2023.The actor and comedian denied the allegations. On Friday, Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations against Brand.Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Sir Mark praised the "bravery" of the women who reported their allegations to police and gave evidence during the trial.He said police would "do everything we can to bring to justice the powerful people who are responsible for probably the most ghastly moment in your life" when sexual assault allegations are made to them.Prime Minister Andy Burnham has been asked about Labour's past association with Brand. Some party figures sought his support more than a decade ago, before police began investigating him.At the time, Brand had gained a following for his left-wing political punditry. Then Labour leader Ed Miliband was interviewed by Brand shortly before the 2015 election, and in 2014 Burnham publicly backed Brand during a row over claims about the comedian's housing arrangements.At the time he said it was "depressing to see media mission to discredit someone who stops playing their game" and urged Brand to "keep going".Speaking on Friday, Burham said: "It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life."He described Brand's crimes as "horrific" and said he had been rightly held to account, adding: "I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing."Brand is being held in custody ahead of his sentencing on Monday.After the jury returned its verdicts, Mr Justice Bennathan told him to expect a "significant custodial term".

schema.headline: Brand's barrister refers himself to regulator after report he confronted journalist

title: New wave of bomb threats hit European airlines
description: A Ryanair flight scheduled to leave Lisbon for Rome on Friday was targeted with a threat, the airline said, while at least 11 flights were targeted in
body: A Ryanair flight scheduled to leave Lisbon for Rome on Friday was targeted with a threat, the airline said, while at least 11 flights were targeted in the Czech Republic and Bulgaria, according to AFP.France also reported at least four of its flights were targeted by threats, however they all landed safely. No explosives have been found on any planes as of Friday. As airlines were dealing with this latest wave of threats, several media outlets, including RTÉ, were evacuated after similar warnings were made against them. Staff at the Irish Independent newspaper and the Dublin offices of radio stations NewstalkFM and TodayFM, were also advised to leave their buildings and UK broadcaster Sky said it also received a security threat.In a statement, gardaí (Irish police) said they were "aware of a threat made against media organisations here and in Europe".While no link has been established between the threats against airlines and media outlets, the Irish government has warned it is a "likely coordinated campaign of disruption".In a statement, it said: "Hoax threats such as these cause fear, distress and disruption to people going about their daily lives and activities; they achieve no positive purpose whatsoever. It is not known yet who is responsible for these threats, whether it is individuals or a centralised or co-ordinated effort.Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin described the situation as "worrying" and added his government's first priority was the safety of the Irish public."Yesterday, there appeared to be coordinated efforts to disrupt air travel," he said.Martin told RTÉ it was not yet known if the threats had come from individuals or if it was a "coordinated attack" but said they were being taken seriously.Ireland is scheduled to host two high-profile European Union meetings in Dublin next week. Broadcaster Sky confirmed it had received a security threat, hours after RTÉ had evacuated its building.The broadcaster, which is owned by Comcast, said in a statement read by a presenter on its news channel that the broadcaster had "carried out a security assessment and reported the matter to the relevant authorities"."The safety and security of our colleagues is our primary concern, and we are working closely with authorities to ensure our people and operations remain secure."Friday's disruption comes after the Russian extremist group "Male State", named in this week's hoax bomb threats to Italian airports, denied any link to the false warnings.Replying to the BBC Russian Service, an account on Telegram - one of several linked to the so-called "Male State" and its founder Vladislav Pozdnyakov - mocked any suggestion the group was involved in emailing the threats."What Male State? Where have you seen it? It hasn't existed for many years," the message on the channel reads. "If tomorrow they sign a [threat] letter, say, from Putin, will you then try to reach our president to ask your stupid question?"

schema.headline: New wave of bomb threats hit European airlines

title: Manhunt in Gloucester after sword incident sparked school lockdowns
description: Police described both suspects as white males. One is aged in his late teens to early 20s, of a medium to large build, and about 6ft tall. He was wear
body: Police described both suspects as white males. One is aged in his late teens to early 20s, of a medium to large build, and about 6ft tall. He was wearing white sliders at the time of the incident.The other suspect is described as being about 5ft 5ins tall, of slim build and wearing black clothing.St Peter's High School pupil Jimmy said the situation was "really scary" and he was still in shock.After getting into the Tuffley school for the day, he said his friends came in and told him something had happened near his home.He said the school's alarm then went off and the computer he was on displayed a message saying "This is a lockdown"."The computers are not accessible at all and we've all had to turn the lights off, lock the doors, turn all the blinds down, and we've had to get on the ground," he said."At the time I was scared. My heart was racing," he added.Jimmy said pupils were locked in their classrooms for two to three hours."[When police cars arrived] I thought this is getting serious, I'm getting worried, I don't know what's going on," he said.The 15-year-old said he was able to message his mother when the school let students use their phones after about an hour."When I was able to eventually get out, she was giving me a bunch of hugs," he said."What I am is shocked. I'm surprised that this happened," he added.Jimmy said the school had previously run lockdown drills but a real event had never happened before.Adam, whose daughter attends the same school, said he felt frightened even though he had texted her and knew she was OK."I don't think this should happen at school. Thank God she is safe," he said.The school had messaged parents to say everything was under control, he added.Another parent outside the school gates earlier, whose daughter is in Year 8 and nephew is in Year 7, said the family was "so worried"."I'm slightly calmer now the police have told us they're safe but I want to take them home. "I haven't heard from them because they aren't allowed phones in school," she added.Addressing parents outside St Peter's High School, an officer said a police presence would remain at the site for the rest of the school day. "That is not there for a safety reason, it is to provide reassurance to yourselves and answer any questions. It is not because there is any risk or threat to anyone," she said.

schema.headline: Manhunt in Gloucester after sword incident sparked school lockdowns

title: Huntingdon train victim says 'this is what it feels like to die'
description: A passenger stabbed multiple times by a knifeman accused of trying to kill 10 people on a train has told jurors he thought "this is what it feels like
body: A passenger stabbed multiple times by a knifeman accused of trying to kill 10 people on a train has told jurors he thought "this is what it feels like to die".Scott Bletcher was on the York to London King's Cross LNER service on 1 November last year when the attacks happened, leading to an unscheduled stop in Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire.On Friday, Cambridge Crown Court also heard from staff member Samir Zitouni, who said he fought back using a frying pan, stating he did not want to "give up until the train stopped".Anthony Williams, 33, of Langford Road, Peterborough, denies 10 counts of attempted murder.He is also charged with four other alleged attempted murders following earlier incidents in Peterborough and London.Bletcher said he was travelling alone after doing Christmas shopping in Newark-on-Trent, in Nottinghamshire, and was "quite looking forward to the tapas I'd bought actually".After Peterborough he noticed people running down the aisle, but he remained seated because he was "still not concerned", presuming there had been a disagreement.He then saw a knife being held in front of him at eye level and said he felt "trapped… there is no way of escape", followed by a "scratch" to the head from the knife.Bletcher said he moved his arm to shield his face and added: "There was nothing said to me and I didn't respond because there was nothing to respond to."The court heard the victim - who is the first to give live evidence at the trial - was stabbed five more times.Passenger Michael Gawthorpe, who was not stabbed by Williams but was in the same carriage as Zitouni, said in a video-recorded interview that he "kept saying calm down, just put the knife down, please stop... we've all got kids".He said Williams said something along the lines of "they're trying to kill me".Gawthorpe recalled someone passing him a large toaster which he said he threw at the attacker.But he said he remembered Williams then looking at him and he thought "that was me done... I thought I've made a mistake here".Another passenger, Christina Jones, wept in her video-recorded interview as she demonstrated how she hid behind her handbag.The court heard she threw a hot drink at Williams.As well as arguing Williams was attempting to murder the 10 people on the train, prosecutors allege that on 31 October he tried to kill three people in Peterborough.He is also charged with attempting to murder a teenager in the early hours of 1 November on a DLR train in east London.Whether Williams carried out the attacks is not in question - the court has been told - but jurors must consider whether he intended to kill.The trial continues.Do you have a story suggestion for Cambridgeshire? Contact us below.

schema.headline: Huntingdon train victim says 'this is what it feels like to die'

title: AI stocks bounce back after trillions wiped from market values
description: Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock val
body: Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index closed in positive territory following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.But the Nasdaq Composite bounced back slightly on Friday, ending the day up 1.1%, partly reversing some of its 5.5% fall. The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, closed up 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was flat through the day before ending slightly down 0.4%.Companies that lost hundreds of billions in market value recovered some ground on Friday, including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla.However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse.The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.The market fluctuations also come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI."The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today."I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."Pierre Baqué, chief executive of AI platform Neural Concept, said the share movements were a "necessary market correction" that reflected a legitimate concern about the amount of money being poured into AI infrastructure."The industry must move beyond unchecked infrastructure investment and demonstrate greater financial discipline," he said. "We are entering a critical transition phase, a market purgatory where raw tech must prove its widespread economic value."Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained."Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."

schema.headline: AI stocks bounce back after trillions wiped from market values

title: Burnham responds to BBC question over Labour's past links to Brand
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Russell Brand has rightly been held to account for his "horrific" crimes and sought to explain Labour's previous
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Russell Brand has rightly been held to account for his "horrific" crimes and sought to explain Labour's previous association with the comedian.Some within the Labour Party attempted to court Brand's support more than a decade ago, before police began investigating him - and in 2014 Burnham posted a supportive message on social media when the comedian was facing media criticism about his housing arrangements.Asked about the 2014 tweet on Friday, Burnham said: "It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life."Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault on Thursday.In 2014, Brand was writing regular opinion pieces for newspapers and appearing on political discussion programmes, including the BBC's Question Time. His anti-establishment and left-wing views had also gained him a following on social media.The same year, Burnham, then the shadow health secretary, posted on Twitter in support of Brand following allegations about the comedian's housing arrangements.It is not clear what Burnham had been referring to in his 2014 tweet, but the previous day, The Sun claimed Brand had paid rent at a property owned by a landlord in a tax haven, while at the same time campaigning against tax avoidance.Brand threatened to sue the newspaper and said he would give the money to victims of the Hillsborough disaster, a group Burnham has long campaigned for.At the time, Burnham said it was "depressing to see media mission to discredit someone who stops playing their game" and urged Brand to "keep going".Asked about that social media post on Friday, Burnham told the BBC "all I can say is I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing or what he went on to do".The PM added: "His [Brand's] crimes are horrific, he's rightly been held to account, justice for the victims and that is the right course that's been taken here."It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life, but what is important is that where there is wrongdoing it is exposed."The prime minister added: "Credit to the victims, huge credit, the courage that it's taken, but also the journalists who've exposed this."Ed Miliband, then the Labour leader, was interviewed by Brand in the run-up to the 2015 general election.Brand, who had previously dismissed the idea of voting, backed Labour following the interview, saying Miliband had convinced him that "this bloke will listen to us".Miliband, who is now foreign secretary, has previously said he regrets being interviewed by Brand. On Friday, a spokesman for Miliband told the BBC: "These are horrific crimes that Russell Brand has been found guilty of and Ed's profound sympathy is with the victims. "As he said in 2023, 'of course, knowing what I know now - and I was not aware of these allegations at the time about Russell Brand - I wouldn't have done that interview and I regret doing it'."Brand was found not guilty of two other counts of rape, and one count of attempted indecent assault.During a four-week trial, Brand faced allegations from six women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009.The 51-year-old was refused bail and will spend the weekend in custody before he is due to return to court on Monday for sentencing.

schema.headline: Burnham responds to BBC question over Labour's past links to Brand

title: Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?
description: While the Trump administration has been all-in on AI, or "super intelligence" as the president likes to call it, many leading Democrats tapped into gr
body: While the Trump administration has been all-in on AI, or "super intelligence" as the president likes to call it, many leading Democrats tapped into grassroots concerns about the expansion of data centres and their impact on local communities.These were largely focused on the facilities' high consumption of water and electricity, which many feared would push up their household bills – as well as the noise, use of land, and general disruption associated with them.A Gallup poll published in May showed 71% of Americans would oppose the building of a data centre in their community. The figure for a nuclear power station was 53%.James Talarico, who won the Senate race in once staunchly Republican Texas, was one of those to respond to this scepticism."While we want to protect America's leadership in artificial intelligence, we are still grappling with how it will affect everything from how we work to how our children learn," he said."We must protect Americans and establish clear, consistent laws for businesses."With control of both houses of Congress, Democrats are now expected to challenge the president's technology agenda more vigorously, while introducing legislation which could curb the expansion of the industry.Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned against data centres, pledging a moratorium on the construction of new facilities.Hinojosa's win could present opposition to tech multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who has moved large parts of SpaceX and Tesla's operations to the state, for years a Republican stronghold.The Tesla boss had spent nearly $450m to back Republican campaigns in the midterms.As the co-founder of the British-based technology firm Arm Holdings, Tudor Brown, points out, "stock values are based on future earnings not present earnings". If the rewards are not likely to be as great as expected, some investors will choose to sell up.The falls seen on stock markets over the past 24 hours would appear to have been triggered by the midterm results. But concerns that tech firms have become overvalued were being expressed long before the elections.The question now is whether this is simply the removal of froth from an over-exuberant market, or a sign that the AI rush is a bubble about to burst, with much wider consequences.Nandini Roy Choudhury of Future Market Insights thinks investors will assess whether the political shift could result in restrictions on data centre construction, energy consumption and the deployment of AI technology.She adds there is unlikely to be an immediate widespread recovery in tech stocks as traders are likely to be more selective, favouring firms with stronger balance sheets.Brown thinks the impact will be limited. Share valuations, he thinks, were inflated by expectations of "almost infinite AI growth", which have been followed by "a bit of a panic"."There is a natural floor to this", he says. "After that it will reflect I think that actually there's still a lot of money being made in these companies".

schema.headline: Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?

title: Judge blocks construction of Donald Trump's massive arch
description: Judge blocks construction of Trump's massive arch after federal agency approvalFigure caption, Watch: Protesters demonstrate against Trump’s proposed
body: Judge blocks construction of Trump's massive arch after federal agency approvalFigure caption, Watch: Protesters demonstrate against Trump’s proposed archByNardine Saad and Isabella JewellReporting fromMemorial CircleUpdated 5 hours agoA federal judge has temporarily blocked construction of US President Donald Trump's "triumphal arch" in the nation's capital.US District Judge Tanya Chutkan ruled that there should be a 14-day pause before any work can start on the arch in Washington which the Trump administration had said could begin this week.  Earlier on Thursday the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) voted 8-4 to allow construction of the planned 250ft (72m) arch. Trump appointees on the board said the arch would be a fitting tribute to US history and to veterans but opponents have argued it would block the view of Arlington National Cemetery, the resting place of thousands of US soldiers and service people. The so-called Arc de Trump - a play on the name of the famous arch in Paris, the Arc de Triomphe - is one of the president's efforts to remake the capital city in his style and is meant to commemorate the country's 250th anniversary.The approval on Thursday evening came after nearly nine hours of public comment."The White House commends the National Capital Planning Commission's decision to fully approve President Trump's historic vision to build a much needed Triumphal Arch in Washington, DC," a White House spokesperson told the BBC in a statement.It is not yet clear  when construction of the arch could begin, as several lawsuits seek to block the project. The White House criticised the federal court that temporarily halted construction as an "activist district court.""We are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds and look forward to seeing the completion of this magnificent Arch," the spokesperson said.Image source, ReutersImage caption, An artist's rendering of Trump's proposed arch near Arlington CemeteryA rendering of the project's design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty statue on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles. The phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" are inscribed in gold on either side of the structure.A website that the White House shared on social media on Friday also shows a video rendering of the arch that shows the structure emblazoned with the words "Golden Age of America" along one side.It refers to the structure as "The Military Triumphal Arch".The proposed structure is sprinkled with appliques that are visually similar to the golden embellishments Trump has added to the Oval Office. The Trump administration has also said the arch would double as a complex to store military equipment - complete with the ability to deploy snipers and drones."There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World," Trump previously wrote on his Truth Social platform. He added that out of "the 59 top cities and Capitals", Washington is "the only one in the world that does not have a triumphal arch". He did not specify to which cities he was referring.Mark Paoletta, the chairman of the NCPC and one of the Trump appointees, said at Thursday's meeting that the president understood "it's important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments". How Trump is remaking the White House in his own imageHe and other commissioners said the structure fulfils a 100-year plan to build a monumental work on Columbia Island, just as Congress and various commissions intended. Paoletta added that the arch would honour the nation, its veterans and "provide the sacred ground of Arlington National Cemetery with the monumental gateway it deserves".Image caption, Anne Wright is among those who are opposed to the archOpponents have strongly disagreed. Anne Wright, who spent 29 years in the US military and also worked in the diplomatic service, told the BBC she would try to stop the construction."We'll tie ourselves to the bulldozer, we've got veterans in wheelchairs and we'll chain the wheelchairs to these things," she said.Wright referenced this week's midterm elections, in which Trump's Republican Party lost control of Congress, saying: "[Trump's] policy of war, of ego – they've been rejected."Fellow veteran John Pomeroy - who served in the Air Force for six years, including during the Vietnam War, and whose parents are buried at Arlington - said the arch "would lessen the solemn nature of a visit to the cemetery".He described Trump's suggestion that the arch could store military equipment as "silly" and a "half-baked idea", arguing it would be a target for terrorist attacks. Like Wright, Pomeroy said he would "impede construction workers as much as I can" if they came to the site to begin work.Democratic Congressman Jared Huffman argued in his statement to the commission that the arch would disrupt sightlines not just of Arlington but of the Lincoln Memorial, fracturing "a view meant to underscore the unity and sacrifice of the American people, and doing that with a structure we often associate with emperors or kings who built grand arches as tributes to themselves". "This is a tribute to Donald Trump," Huffman added.Lawsuits have been filed against the plans, raising concerns about the environment, traffic congestion and safety. There is also a disagreement over whether congressional approval is needed to build the arch. It is one of several construction projects Trump has proposed for the US capital. That includes at the White House, where he is facing legal challenges over the construction of a ballroom, which is estimated to cost $400m (£300m). His plans to renovate a 106-year-old golf course, which he has dubbed "trash island", is also being challenged in the courts.Rebecka Pieder contributed reporting.

schema.headline: Judge blocks construction of Donald Trump's massive arch
